_comment: Two-minute pronunciation warm-ups shown on speaking days. audioUrl is a pattern; {word} is replaced by each word. Read each word aloud, then compare with a native speaker.

drills.title: Nasal vowels: an/en vs on
drills.tip: [ɑ̃] (an, en, am, em) is open, mouth wide, tongue low. [ɔ̃] (on, om) has rounded lips. Don't add an n or ng at the end.

drills.title: Nasal vowels: in/ain vs an
drills.tip: [ɛ̃] (in, ain, ein, im, un) is a nasal è with spread lips. In modern French, un sounds the same as in.

drills.title: Nasal or not? bon / bonne
drills.tip: A vowel + n/m is nasal only when no vowel follows. Bonne, une, ami: the n is pronounced and the vowel is NOT nasal.

drills.title: u [y] vs ou [u]
drills.tip: For u, say i and round your lips without moving your tongue. Spanish and English don't have this sound.

drills.title: é vs è vs e
drills.tip: é (and -er, -ez) is closed, smile. è/ê/ai is open. Unaccented e in le, de, je is a short, relaxed [ə] and often disappears.

drills.title: Silent endings: -ent, -s, -t, -x, -d
drills.tip: Final consonants are usually silent (except often c, r, f, l: think CaReFuL). The verb ending -ent is never pronounced: ils parlent = il parle.

drills.title: Liaison and enchaînement
drills.tip: A silent final consonant is pronounced before a vowel in fixed groups: les_amis [z], un_enfant [n], petit_ami [t]. Never after et.

drills.title: eu: closed [ø] vs open [œ]
drills.tip: Closed [ø] at the end of a syllable (deux, peu); open [œ] before a pronounced consonant (peur, sœur). Both have rounded lips.

drills.title: The French R
drills.tip: Made at the back of the throat, like a soft gargle; not the Spanish tapped or rolled r. Start with gr, tr, then final -re.

drills.title: Spelling vs sound: oi, ai, au, eau, gn, ill
drills.tip: oi = [wa], ai = [ɛ], au/eau = [o], gn = [ɲ] (like Spanish ñ), ill = [j] (mostly).
